newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Inaugural oath takes seconds, party lasts for days.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Inaugural oath takes seconds, party lasts for days.

text.p: It will take Bill Clinton only about 45 seconds to repeat the oath of office and be sworn in for a second term as president, but there are days of celebrations surrounding the simple ceremony at the Capitol.

Long gone are the days when a president can ride up to Capitol Hill for his inaugural virtually alone, as Thomas Jefferson did in 1801. Clinton's second inauguration will be big and brash, replete with fireworks, star perforers, lavish dinners, crowded streets, sober lectures, champagne galas, expensive gowns and even Elmo, a lovable children's monster.

It will not be as big as Clinton's first inaugural in 1993. Second inaugurals are typically less bombastic, but inaugural committee chairman Terence McAuliffe boasted, "We will have more people than ever at the second inauguration of an American president."

The festivities for the 53rd presidential inauguration run from Saturday through Monday with the theme "An American Journey: Building a Bridge to the 21st Century." That span was oft-cited by Clinton in his campaign against Republican Bob Dole, and it is back with a fresh coat of paint.

"We're talking about the fact that this is the last inauguration of the 20th century and we're wanting to be a little more reflective and think about how we've gotten here and where we go next," inaugural spokesman David Seldin said. "It's also a confirmation, not so much of the fact that Bill Clinton was re-elected but of American democracy, that once again the constitutional process of elections is working."
Democracy means freedom and there are plenty of inaugural events that are free, but it is best to keep in mind the capitalist idea that the more money one has, the better time one is likely to have.

On Saturday and Sunday the masses can go on a free musical and oratorical tour, in huge tents set up on the Mall, of such subjects as the Revolutionary War, which won independence from Britain, Native American dances and slavery.

They can hear talks from famous people such as Holocaust survivor and Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel and feminist Betty Friedan. And there is a full programme for children, which is where Elmo, the red critter from the Sesame Street television show, will entertain.

Musicial events feature the big band sound of the Count Basie Orchestra, 1960s folk music from Peter, Paul and Mary, and Irish tunes from Celtic Thunder. For the taste buds there are regional delicacies such as clam chowder and fried green tomatoes. Fireworks erupt at dusk on Saturday.

About 11,000 people were invited to attend a huge gala on Sunday night at ticket prices up to $3,000 apiece. Clinton and his wife Hillary are to attend and the stars will come out to perform -- Gloria Estefan, Michael Douglas, Whoopi Goldberg, Aretha Franklin, Kenny G, Stevie Wonder and many more.

Washington will stand still at 11:30 a.m. (1630 GMT) on Monday when Clinton is sworn in on the steps of the Capitol, but will rollick anew with the post-inaugural parade of floats and marching bands down Pennsylvania Avenue to the White House. Look for the Tigers on Wheels Unicycle Team from Warrensville Heights, Ohio, or the proud mules of Arkansan Joe "Rasputin" Huie.
Crowds standing on the street can watch for free. It costs $10 to $100 for a seat in the stands set up along the route.

Yards of satin will swish through the streets when various inaugural balls get under way on Monday night. Hillary Rodham Clinton will be wearing an Oscar de la Renta creation, while Vice President Al Gore's wife Tipper will have on a Kay Unger.
"The dress Mrs. Gore selected enhances her classic beauty, establishing a sophisticated, yet very feminine image to begin the presidential term," said an Unger statement.

Name a subject and there may be a ball for it: The Black Tie and Boots gala for Texans, the Medal of Honours Recipients ball for war veterans, the Asian Pacific Americans Ball, the Gay and Lesbian Inaugural Ball, and on and on.

Some hotels were hoping to entice high-dollar attendees into "special deals." The Ritz-Carlton offered a four-night, $30,000 package for its presidential suite with 24-hour butler service, a chauffeur, breakfast in bed, champagne and caviar.
"There is something for everyone at the inauguration, and it is as much or as little as you want," Hillary Clinton's spokesman, Neel Lattimore, said. "It is fundamentally a great American tradition."
